t: Strange Printer II - Bounding Boxes Boil Down to Topological Order
o:
## Understanding the problem

The printer stamps one solid single-color rectangle per turn, later stamps overwrite earlier ones, and each color may be used at most once. We must decide whether some order of stamps reproduces targetGrid exactly.

Reasoning backwards is the key move: whichever color is stamped last must appear, in the final picture, as a clean rectangle of its own color - any foreign pixel inside its bounding box would still be visible. In example 1, color 2 occupies a tidy box, so it can be stamped last with color 1 filling the frame first: true. Example 3 is a checkerboard of 1s and 2s; each color's bounding box spans the whole grid and contains the other color, so neither can go last, and indeed no order works.

Formally, compute each color's bounding box and add an edge c -> d whenever a cell of color d lies inside c's box: c must be printed before d so that d can overwrite it there. The grid is printable exactly when this digraph is acyclic, which Kahn's algorithm decides instantly at these sizes (60 x 60 grid, at most 60 colors).
k: Work backwards: a color eligible to be stamped last has a bounding box containing no cells of any other color.
Every foreign cell inside color c's box forces the edge c -> d, since d must be stamped after c to overwrite that cell.
Feasibility equals acyclicity of the dependency graph; equivalently, repeatedly peel off any color whose box currently shows only its own color.

a.i: Enumerate every permutation of the colors, stamp each color's full bounding rectangle in that order onto a blank grid, and compare against the target. This is the problem statement made executable and is trivially correct, but with up to 60 colors the factorial search is purely theoretical - useful only as a correctness reference for tiny inputs.
s: Compute each used color's bounding box from the grid.
Iterate over all permutations of the used colors.
Repaint a blank grid by stamping each color's rectangle in permutation order.
Accept if some permutation reproduces targetGrid exactly.
a.t: O(k! * k * m * n) - factorial many orders, each simulated across the grid.
a.sp: O(m * n) - the scratch grid per simulation.

a.n: Approach 2: Dependency Graph and Topological Sort
a.i: Bounding boxes turn the puzzle into scheduling: if any cell of color d falls inside color c's bounding box, then c must be stamped strictly before d or the final picture would show c there instead of d. Build that graph by scanning each color's box for resident foreign colors, then run Kahn's algorithm. Processing every color certifies a valid stamping order exists; a leftover cycle proves impossibility. This is the intended solution and runs in well under a millisecond at the given limits.
s: Record the min/max row and column seen for each color.
For each color c, scan its box, collect resident colors, and add edge c -> d for every other color found, incrementing indegrees.
Seed a worklist with all indegree-0 colors.
Pop a color, decrement successors' indegrees, enqueue zeros.
Return whether every used color was processed.
a.t: O(C * m * n + E) - each color scans its own box once; C <= 60 colors.
a.sp: O(C^2) - adjacency sets over at most 60 colors dominate storage.

w: Lead with the reverse-peeling intuition, then formalize it as a topological sort - showing you can convert a geometric story into a graph is what interviewers reward. Pitfalls: getting the edge direction backwards (ask who must print earlier so the final pixels win), forgetting that a box legitimately containing only its own color contributes no edges, and assuming merely adjacent or overlapping rectangles interact - only actual containment of foreign cells matters. Edge cases: single-color grids (trivially true), colors occupying one cell. Likely follow-ups: minimize the number of operations, or allow color reuse, which breaks cycles and needs a different feasibility argument.
